summary: Describes a framework for supporting IETF Integrated Services on shared and switched IEEE 802 LAN infrastructure. It sets out the concepts that companion documents use for admission control and service mapping. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo is the plan for offering guaranteed quality of service on office and campus networks. It describes the functions a network needs, such as deciding whether a new stream can be accommodated, and divides them between software that runs on each computer and a component that keeps track of what has been promised. It then looks at how each kind of LAN hardware could carry the result.

questions: qos on shared and switched lans
how to support quality of service on local networks
integrated services over ethernet and token ring
subtitle: A framework for giving some traffic a reserved share of a local network, using the priority mechanisms that LAN hardware already has.

tldr.problem: Local area networks offer best-effort delivery only, and they have no way to reserve capacity, schedule queues or police traffic. Simply running the IETF reservation protocol over an Ethernet segment achieves nothing, because the link layer has no admission control.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a Bandwidth Manager made of a Requester Module in each end station and a Bandwidth Allocator that makes the admission decisions, with signalling protocols between them. Switches map the reserved service onto the priority levels their hardware already supports, which on Token Ring means eight levels and on plain Ethernet only two.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and is a framework rather than a protocol. Companion memos cover the signalling protocol and the mapping of services onto link-layer priority, and the memo's security section says the model creates no known new avenues for malicious attack.

facts.label: IP MTU over LLC/SNAP on Ethernet

today: RFC 2816 is an Informational memo from May 2000 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a framework, not a protocol: the signalling protocol and the mapping of services onto link-layer priority are in companion memos from the same working group, and the memo says that because the framework is meant to be exhaustive, not every function it describes may be supportable on a particular topology or technology.

sections.title: Why Local Networks Need Their Own Resource Management
sections.content:
The Internet has traditionally provided support for best-effort traffic only. With advances in link layer technology and with emerging real-time applications such as video conferencing and Internet telephony, there has been much interest in developing mechanisms that enable real-time services over the Internet. A framework for meeting these new requirements was set out in RFC 1633, and that has driven the specification of various classes of network service by the Integrated Services working group, such as Controlled Load and Guaranteed Service. Each of these service classes provides a certain quality of service to traffic conforming to a specified set of parameters, and applications are expected to choose one of these classes according to their requirements.

One mechanism for end stations to use such services in an IP network is the Resource Reservation Protocol, RFC 2205, developed by the RSVP working group of the IETF. The IEEE under its Project 802 has defined standards for many different local area network technologies. These all typically offer the same MAC layer datagram service to higher layer protocols such as IP, although they often provide different dynamic behaviour characteristics, and it is these that matter when considering their ability to support real-time services. IEEE 802 has also defined standards for bridging multiple LAN segments together using devices known as MAC bridges or switches, and recent work has defined traffic classes, multicast filtering and virtual LAN capabilities for these devices.

Such LAN technologies often constitute the last hops between users and the Internet, as well as being a primary building block for entire campus networks, so it is necessary to provide standardized mechanisms for using them to support end-to-end real-time services. In order to do this there must be some mechanism for resource management at the data link layer. Resource management in this context encompasses the functions of admission control, scheduling, traffic policing and so on, and the ISSLL, Integrated Services over Specific Link Layers, working group in the IETF was chartered with the purpose of exploring and standardizing such mechanisms for various link layer technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Office and campus networks are usually the last hop before the Internet, so a promise about delay or bandwidth has to hold on them too. But a switch in a local network has no notion of a reservation, no way to refuse a new stream, and usually only one or two priority queues. This memo works out what a local network would have to add, and where in the standardisation process that belongs.

sections.title: How IEEE 802 Networks Carry Priority
sections.content:
The user_priority is a value associated with the transmission and reception of all frames in the IEEE 802 service model. It is supplied by the sender using the MAC service and provided along with the data to the receiver, and it may or may not actually be carried over the network. Token Ring, IEEE 802.5, carries the value encoded in its frame control octet, while basic Ethernet, IEEE 802.3, does not carry it. IEEE 802.12 may or may not carry it depending on the frame format in use. When the IEEE 802.3 frame format is used, only the two levels of priority, high and low, that are used to determine access priority can be recovered, based on the value of priority encoded in the start delimiter of the IEEE 802.3 frame.

IEEE 802.1D defines a consistent way of carrying the value of user_priority over a bridged network consisting of Ethernet, Token Ring, Demand Priority, FDDI or other MAC layer media, using an extended frame format. If the user_priority is carried explicitly in packets, its utility is as a simple label enabling packets within a data stream in different classes to be discriminated easily by downstream nodes without having to parse the packet in more detail. An explicit field also means desktop and wiring closet switches do not have to change hardware or software as the rules for classifying packets evolve.

IEEE 802.1D defines static priority queuing as the default mode of operation of switches that implement multiple queues, but the user_priority is only a priority in a loose sense, since it depends on the number of traffic classes actually implemented by a switch. The user_priority is defined as a 3 bit quantity with a value of 7 representing the highest priority and a value of 0 as the lowest. Packets are queued within a particular traffic class based on the received user_priority, obtained directly from the packet if an IEEE 802.1Q header or an IEEE 802.5 network is used, or assigned according to some local policy. The queue is selected by a mapping from user_priority, 0 through 7, onto the number of available traffic classes, and a switch may implement one or more traffic classes. The advertised IntServ parameters and the switch's admission control behaviour may be used to determine that mapping. A switch is not precluded from implementing other scheduling algorithms such as weighted fair queuing and round robin.
sections.plainLanguage: The 802 standards have a small priority number, three bits, running from 0 to 7, and each switch maps that number onto however many queues it actually has. A switch with two queues uses 0 to 3 for one and 4 to 7 for the other, say, while a switch with eight queues uses each number for its own queue. Token Ring carries the number in the frame, so it survives the trip; plain Ethernet does not, so the number has to be guessed again at every switch.

sections.title: What the Mechanism Must Do
sections.content:
The memo lists the requirements a mechanism for Integrated Services in a LAN has to meet.

  • Resource reservation. The mechanism must be capable of reserving resources on a single segment or multiple segments and at the bridges and switches connecting them. It must be able to provide reservations for both unicast and multicast sessions, and it should be possible to change the level of reservation while the session is in progress.
  • Admission control. The mechanism must be able to estimate the level of resources necessary to meet the quality of service requested by the session, in order to decide whether the session can be admitted. For the purpose of management it is useful to be able to respond to queries about availability of resources, and it must be able to make admission control decisions for different types of service such as Guaranteed Service and Controlled Load.
  • Flow separation and scheduling. It is necessary to provide a mechanism for traffic flow separation so that real-time flows can be given preferential treatment over best-effort flows, and their packets can then be isolated and scheduled according to their service requirements.
  • Policing and shaping. Traffic must be shaped or policed by end stations to ensure conformance to negotiated traffic parameters, and shaping is the recommended behaviour for traffic sources. This is because bridges and switches are not typically capable of maintaining the per-flow state that would be required to check flows for conformance. Policing is left as an option for bridges and switches.
  • Soft state. The mechanism must maintain soft state information about the reservations, which means state information must be periodically refreshed if the reservation is to be maintained, or the state and the corresponding reservation will expire after a pre-specified interval.
  • Centralized or distributed implementation. In a centralized implementation a single entity manages the resources of the entire subnet, which is easier to deploy since bridges and switches may not need to be upgraded, but scales poorly with the geographical size of the subnet and the number of end stations attached. In a fully distributed implementation each segment has a local entity managing its resources, which scales better but requires that all bridges and switches in the network support new mechanisms. A semi-distributed implementation is also possible, with more than one entity each managing a subset of segments and switches.
  • Scalability. The mechanism and protocols should have a low overhead and should scale to the largest receiver groups likely to occur within a single link layer domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is the shopping list for a local quality-of-service mechanism. It has to be able to hold capacity aside for a stream, say no when there is not enough, keep real-time packets apart from ordinary ones, check that senders stick to their rate, refresh the promise periodically so it does not survive a crash, and work whether one machine keeps the books or every switch does.

sections.title: The Bandwidth Manager
sections.content:
The resource management functions are provided by an entity called the Bandwidth Manager, which has three parts.

The Requester Module (RM) resides in every end station in the subnet. One of its functions is to provide an interface between applications or higher layer protocols such as RSVP, and the Bandwidth Manager. To initiate a reservation, the following parameters must be passed to it: the service desired, Guaranteed Service or Controlled Load; the traffic descriptors contained in the TSpec; and an RSpec specifying the amount of resources to be reserved. The network layer addresses of the end points must also be specified. The Requester Module must then translate the network layer addresses into link layer addresses and convert the request into a format understood by the components responsible for admission control. It is also responsible for returning the status of requests processed by the Bandwidth Manager to the invoking application or higher layer protocol.

The Bandwidth Allocator (BA) is responsible for performing admission control and maintaining state about the allocation of resources in the subnet. An end station can request various services, such as a bandwidth reservation, the modification of an existing reservation, or queries about resource availability, and these requests are processed by the Bandwidth Allocator. The communication between the end station and the Bandwidth Allocator takes place through the Requester Module. The Bandwidth Allocator is also responsible for deciding how to label flows: based on the admission control decision it may indicate to the Requester Module that packets belonging to a particular flow should be tagged with some priority value which maps to the appropriate traffic class.

Three communication protocols are needed. Between the higher layer protocols and the Requester Module, the Bandwidth Manager must define primitives for the application to initiate reservations, query the Bandwidth Allocator about available resources, and change or delete reservations. Between the Requester Module and the Bandwidth Allocator, a signalling mechanism must be defined. And between peer Bandwidth Allocators, if there is more than one in the subnet, a means must be specified for inter-allocator communication: the allocators must be able to decide among themselves which one is responsible for which segments and switches, must be able to handle a request for a reservation along the domain of multiple allocators, and their communication will also be responsible for back-up and recovery in the event of failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The Bandwidth Manager has two kinds of part. A small piece sits in every computer and acts as the contact point, translating what the application asked for into something the network can act on. The other part is the decision maker, which keeps the record of what has been promised and says yes or no. When several decision makers are used, they also have to talk to each other about who is responsible for which part of the network.

sections.title: Admission Control at a Switch
sections.content:
On receipt of an admission control request, a switch performs a sequence of steps, using the Subnet Bandwidth Manager as an example. The behaviour depends on whether the designated manager for that segment is within this switch.

If the ingress manager is the designated one for the link, it either translates the received user_priority or selects a Layer 2 traffic class that appears compatible with the request and whose use does not violate any administrative policies in force. In effect it matches the requested service with the available traffic classes and chooses the best one, and it ensures that the user_priority corresponding to that traffic class is passed back to the client if the reservation succeeds. The designated manager then observes the current state of allocation of resources on the input port or link and determines whether the new resource allocation from the mapped traffic class can be accommodated. If it is accepted, the request is passed to the reservation propagator. If the ingress manager is not the designated one for the link, it passes the request straight on to the propagator.

The reservation propagator relays the request to the bandwidth accountants on each of the switch's outbound links to which the reservation would apply, which implies an interface to the routing and forwarding database. Each egress bandwidth accountant observes the current state of allocation of queuing resources on its outbound port and of bandwidth on the link itself, and determines whether the new allocation can be accommodated. This is only a local decision at this switch hop: further Layer 2 hops through the network may veto the request as it passes along.

If accepted, the request is propagated on each output link selected, and any user_priority in the forwarded request must be translated according to any egress mapping table. The switch must then notify the client of the user_priority to be used for packets belonging to that flow. This is an optimistic approach that assumes admission control succeeds; downstream switches may still refuse the request. If the switch wishes to reject the request, it can do so by notifying the client that originated it by means of its Layer 2 address.
sections.plainLanguage: When a reservation request reaches a switch, the switch first matches the service asked for against the traffic classes it actually implements and picks the closest one, then checks whether its own input port and each of its output ports have room for what was asked. If everything fits, it tells the client which priority value to use and passes the request on. If it does not fit, it says no, and a later switch along the path may also say no even if this one said yes.

sections.title: Summary and Security
sections.content:
The memo has specified a framework for providing Integrated Services over shared and switched LAN technologies. The ability to provide quality of service guarantees necessitates some form of admission control and resource management. The requirements and goals of a resource management scheme for subnets have been identified and discussed, and the entire scheme is referred to as a Bandwidth Manager. Architectural considerations were discussed and examples provided to illustrate possible implementations, and some of the issues involved in mapping the services from higher layers to the link layer were also discussed. Accompanying memos from the ISSLL working group address service mapping issues and provide a protocol specification for the Bandwidth Manager protocol based on the requirements and goals discussed in this document.

Two mapping questions are worth naming. The traffic class used by a flow should depend on the quality of service desired and on whether the reservation succeeded, so a sender should use the user_priority value that maps to the best effort traffic class until the Bandwidth Manager tells it otherwise after a successful reservation. And for traffic from sources that exceed their negotiated contract, the controlled load service recommends dropping the excess rather than re-mapping it to a lower priority, because re-ordering problems may make that undesirable, particularly for flows using TCP.

The security section says that implementation of the model described creates no known new avenues for malicious attack on the network infrastructure, and refers readers to section 2.8 of the RSVP specification for a discussion of the impact of admission control signalling protocols on network security.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo's closing position is that the hard part is not the machinery but the mapping: a service promise has to be turned into a priority number that the hardware understands, and a sender must not assume it has a good priority until the network has confirmed the reservation. As for security, the framework adds nothing new, and the reservation protocol's own security discussion is the place to look.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN REQUIREMENTS FOR A LAN RESOURCE MECHANISM (RFC 2816)

items.title: Resource reservation
items.text: Hold capacity on one or more segments, for unicast or multicast, and change it later.

items.title: Admission control
items.text: Estimate the resources needed and decide whether the session can be admitted.

items.title: Flow separation and scheduling
items.text: Give real-time flows preferential treatment over best-effort flows.

items.title: Policing and shaping
items.text: End stations shape their traffic to the negotiated parameters.

items.title: Soft state
items.text: Reservations must be refreshed periodically or they expire.

items.title: Centralized or distributed
items.text: One manager for the subnet, or a local one on each segment.

items.title: Scalability
items.text: Low overhead, scaling to the largest receiver groups in a domain.
